title: Diodes and capacitors for the transport of monopoles in fragmented spin ice
authors: Anoop Raj, Sumiran Pujari, Ludovic D. C. Jaubert
abstract: Spin-ice materials are famous for their quasi-particle excitations that behave like magnetic monopoles. Magnetricity is the concept that these monopoles can conduct an AC magnetic current, in analogy with conduction electrons. While monopole dynamics has been intensively studied and is reasonably well understood, very little has been done to design devices in order to control magnetricity. Here we develop a theoretical proof of concept for the design of diodes and capacitors for the transport of monopoles. We use the property of systems with magnetic fragmentation, where spin-ice physics co-exists with long-range antiferromagnetic order. The key point is that magnetic order allows for the existence of domain walls. Under certain conditions of preparation, this domain wall is equivalent to an asymmetric filter for monopoles. In a given direction, positive charges can go through while negative ones are repelled; the opposite applies in the opposite direction. This asymmetry effectively functions like a diode for monopole current. Successive domain walls separate positive from negative charges with a vacuum of charge in between, producing a capacitor for monopoles. Once the capacitor is charged, it can in principle be used as a battery for monopoles. All microscopic mechanisms are explained and our proof of concept is validated by simulations of more than a million spins. Application to experiments are discussed for rare-earth pyrochlore oxides and artificial spin ice. Finally, we discuss in general terms how a domain wall in fragmented spin ice can also be seen as an emergent boundary separating two mirror "worlds" separated by time-reversal symmetry. Beyond spin ice, our work opens a promising direction of investigation for the dynamics of emergent quasi-particles crossing domain walls in chiral and nematic spin liquids, which also possess a broken symmetry.
summary: This paper develops a theoretical framework showing how domain walls within magnetically fragmented spin ice can be engineered to function as functional components like diodes and capacitors for transporting magnetic monopoles. By leveraging the asymmetry inherent in these domain walls, the authors propose a novel method to control monopole current, opening avenues for designing quantum-like electronic devices based on frustrated magnetism.
main_problem: The primary goal is to design theoretical concepts for electronic/magnetic devices, specifically diodes and capacitors, that utilize the transport properties of magnetic monopoles in spin-ice materials.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that domain walls formed in magnetically fragmented spin ice act as an asymmetric filter (diode) for monopole current, and successive walls can accumulate charge to form a capacitor.
method: The work combines theoretical proof of concept with extensive numerical simulations involving over a million spins to validate the predicted monopole transport mechanisms.
model_or_system: The system is based on spin-ice materials exhibiting magnetic fragmentation, where quasi-particles behave as magnetic monopoles. The physics incorporates long-range antiferromagnetic order leading to domain walls separating different local orders (D and $\bar{D}$).
key_observables: Directional asymmetry of monopole current (diode effect), charge accumulation across domain walls (capacitor formation), and the resulting AC magnetic current ('magnetricity').
important_parameters: The existence and structure of domain walls, which are crucial for inducing directional bias; the material type (e.g., pyrochlore oxides).
main_assumptions: It is assumed that the domain wall remains immobile during monopole transport simulations, allowing monopoles to pass through while establishing asymmetry.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the magnetic fragmentation on the lattice, showing how flipping spins creates domain walls. Subsequent figures detail the diode effect by comparing probability distributions of positive vs. negative charges crossing the interface, and show the microscopic mechanism for charge reflection or transmission.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical context (monopoles in spin ice), introduces the concept of magnetic fragmentation leading to domain walls, theoretically proves that these walls act as diodes/capacitors, validates this with large-scale simulations, and concludes by discussing broader implications for other chiral or nematic spin liquids.
why_interesting: The work provides a concrete, device-oriented application (diodes/capacitors) to the complex physics of emergent quasi-particles in frustrated magnets, linking topological defects (domain walls) directly to electronic functionality. This bridges fundamental condensed matter theory with solid-state device concepts.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Fragmentation in spin ice and domain walls: The pyrochlore lattice is made of corner-sharing tetrahedra with four spin sublattices, one at each tetrahedron corner. The centres of all tetrahedra form a bipartite diamond lattice. (a) In a fragmented Coulomb phase, all tetrahedra are for example in a 3in-1out state on up tetrahedra (blue) and a 3out-1in state on down tetrahedra (red), defined as domain D. Flipping all spins around a closed loop of in-out-in-out... spins preserves the domain D (see green hexagon) (b) Flipping all spins in the system corresponds to domain ¯D. (c) The magnetic degrees of freedom of a 3in-1out state can be decomposed into two parts [19]: (i) a 4in,...

Figure 2: Domain walls in fragmented spin ice: (a) Starting from a fragmented spin configuration in domain D, we define a (green) plane at layer z = ndw, orthogonal to the [001] direction. (b) Flipping all spins above this plane transforms the upper part of the system from domain D to ¯D. The domain wall is one-tetrahedron layer thick, where 3out-1in and 3in-1out states co-exist; the former (red) belong to the lower domain D, while the latter (blue) belong to upper domain ¯D.

Figure 3: Diode effect: (a) Schematic representation of the system divided into domains D (bottom) and ¯D (top) via a domain wall at z = ndw = L/2. (b,c) Probability distribution function of the position of monopole carriers, as a function of z, during their diffusion in presence of a domain wall, for negative (b) and positive (c) charges. Simulation details are given in appendix A. (d,e) Microscopic mechanism of the diode effect. Starting from a given initial state at the domain wall, the green paths illustrates how (d) a negative charge is reflected, while (e) a positive charge can be transmitted. Coming from below, this interface is a W+ domain wall.

Figure 4: Capacitor: (a) Schematic representation of the system with p domain walls, ensuring that positive charges can only go up while negative ones can only go down. A single pair of charges is created in the central region, and its evolution is tracked under Monte Carlo dynamics. (b) Distribution of the position of positive (blue) and negative (red) charges along the z−axis, as a function of simulation time for p = 28 domain walls and L = 256. Solid lines represent the average over all independent runs, while thin light-coloured ones correspond to individual runs. The vertical axis denotes the domain index i = {−14, ..., 0, ..., +14}. The horizontal axis is shown on a logarithmic scale....
